name: Weston A. Price diet

lead: The Weston A. Price diet is a traditional-foods approach based on dentist Weston A. Price's 1939 book comparing the teeth and faces of traditional and Westernised peoples. Followers aim for sound teeth and a well-developed jaw and face.

The central claim is that nutrient-dense traditional foods support normal tooth and jaw development, while refined sugar, flour and processed fats cause deficiency and decay. This rests on Price's observational comparisons; his book drew early praise and later criticism for lacking quantitative analysis and control groups. No clinical trials of the diet as a whole were found.

paras: People eat whole traditional foods such as raw or full-fat dairy, eggs, organ meats, bone broths and fermented foods, and cut refined flour, sugar and industrial vegetable fats. It is a long-term eating pattern, often applied from childhood or pregnancy by those who follow it.
No specific harms were identified in the sources reviewed. Critics focus on the observational basis of Price's surveys and on his earlier focal infection theory, which later reviews discredited.

angle.text: Followers eat traditional whole foods and avoid refined flour and sugar, aiming for better dental and jaw development and a wider, healthier-looking face. The idea comes from a 1930s dentist's comparisons of teeth and faces across populations; the diet itself has not been trialled.

lead: The Weston A. Price diet is a traditional-foods way of eating drawn from dentist Weston A. Price (1870-1948), who compared the diets, teeth and facial development of traditional and Westernised populations in his 1939 book Nutrition and Physical Degeneration [1]. Followers say nutrient-dense whole foods support well-formed teeth and jaws, and that refined flour, sugar and industrial vegetable fats are linked to dental decay and poorer facial development, a theme that appeals to people interested in jaw and face structure.

The Weston A. Price Foundation, co-founded in 1999 by Sally Fallon and Mary G. Enig, promotes raw milk, animal fats such as lard, tallow and cod liver oil, lacto-fermented foods, bone broths and minimally processed or soaked grains [1][2]. Lifters on T Nation have cited Price when arguing for low-carbohydrate high-fat eating, animal foods and raw dairy [3][4].

Price's work was received with both praise and criticism, and critics have faulted the lack of quantitative dietary analysis and control groups [1]. No clinical trials of the diet as a whole were found.

paras: Price was born in Ontario in 1870, qualified in dentistry at the University of Michigan in 1893 and practised in Cleveland, Ohio. He chaired the National Dental Association between 1914 and 1928 and worked on dental radiography and porcelain furnace technology.[1]

He first studied dental disease through the lens of focal infection, arguing that infected and root-treated teeth could cause systemic illness. That theory later fell out of favour, and reviews in 1940 and 1951 criticised the methods behind it.[1] Around the 1920s he turned to nutrition, and Nutrition and Physical Degeneration (1939) compared groups including Swiss Alpine villagers, Native American, Polynesian, Pygmy and Aboriginal peoples, using many photographs.[1]

Price argued that Western diseases were rare among traditional peoples and rose as they adopted commercially processed foods, and he blamed refined flour, sugar and modern processed vegetable fats for deficiency, tooth decay and poor facial development.[1] Later organisations built dietary recommendations on these ideas; the Weston A. Price Foundation was co-founded in 1999 by Sally Fallon and Mary G. Enig.[1]

The Weston A. Price Foundation advocates access to certified raw milk, traditional fats such as lard, tallow, cod liver oil and olive oil, lacto-fermented dairy and vegetables such as sauerkraut, and bone stocks. It recommends unprocessed or minimally processed and organic foods and whole grains that are soaked or soured to reduce phytic acid and other anti-nutrients [2]. It takes a favourable view of saturated fat and opposes the lipid hypothesis [2].

A 1940 Canadian Medical Association Journal review called the book a masterpiece of research, and a 1950 Laryngoscope review compared Price to Charles Darwin. Other reviewers said some conclusions went beyond the evidence, and JAMA described him as observant but not wholly unbiased.[1]

A 1981 critique by William T. Jarvis argued that Price held a preconceived view of primitive health, lacked quantitative dietary analysis and overlooked malnutrition, high infant mortality and gum disease. Stephen Barrett, a consumer-health critic, likewise described Price's survey as superficial. The Weston A. Price Foundation has published a rebuttal.[1]

Quackwatch has called the foundation's dietary strategies questionable and Science-Based Medicine criticised its website, and Joel Fuhrman faulted it for not updating recommendations in light of contrary evidence [2]. An FDA official described its raw milk claims as false and unsupported, and the CDC and FDA state that pasteurization does not significantly change milk's nutritional value [2]. The foundation says it receives no government or agribusiness funding [2].
No studies found. The historical literature consists of Price's own observational surveys and later commentary, such as a 1950 Swiss journal article reviewing his work on diet and dental disease.[5]
